content:
03-Schizophrenia

Schizophrenia

In one sentence: A chronic severe mental disorder centred on psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions and thought disorder, with lifetime prevalence about 1% and peak male onset at 15–24; diagnosis uses ICD-10 subtypes or DSM-5 symptom criteria plus six months' duration, treatment centres firmly on antipsychotics (ECT for catatonia, clozapine for resistance), prognosis follows a “rule of quarters,” and cardiovascular disease rather than suicide is the leading contributor to mortality.

Key Points

• Schizophrenia derives from Greek for “split mind,” referring to divided mental functions, not dissociative identity disorder, popularly called multiple personality. Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler coined it in 1908; Kraepelin previously called the illness dementia praecox.

• Psychosis means experiences/beliefs without a basis in reality. Its principal phenomena are hallucinations (sensory perceptions without corresponding stimuli, most commonly auditory in psychosis) and delusions (false fixed beliefs held absolutely, not shared by family/cultural group). Schizophrenic delusions are mainly persecutory, sometimes grandiose.

• Schneider's eleven first-rank symptoms are no longer considered diagnostic because they occur in other psychotic disorders, but strongly suggest schizophrenia when present.

• ICD-10 divides schizophrenia into paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic and simple subtypes, with respective minimum durations of one month, one month, two weeks and one year. DSM-5 removes subtypes, renames the category “schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders,” and requires at least two of five symptoms, one from the first three, and at least six months' duration.

• Lifetime prevalence is about 1%, annual incidence about 2/1000, male:female ratio about 1.4:1. Male onset peaks at 15–24; women begin about 5–10 years later and have a second peak.

• No single causal gene exists; inheritance is probably polygenic, many genes each contributing small effects, shared with depression, bipolar disorder and autism. Genetic risk is neither necessary nor sufficient: population risk 1%, identical twins 50%, first-degree relatives 10%.

• The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome) is the only established genetic subtype, accounting for only 1% of cases.

• Antipsychotics are the treatment mainstay: “start low, go slow,” adequate doses for at least 4–6 weeks. Onset generally takes 2–3 weeks, peak another 2–3. Continue at least one year after remission; maintenance by episode count is one/two/five years.

• Clozapine is preferred for treatment resistance (at least two adequate antipsychotic trials unsuccessful, affecting about 20–30%). About 1% develop agranulocytosis, requiring regular white-cell/neutrophil monitoring; it also has anti-suicide effects. The lecture gives catatonic schizophrenia as the sole ECT indication in schizophrenia.

• The old “rule of thirds” becomes a “rule of quarters”: 25% fully recover without long-term treatment, 25% improve substantially and live independently, 25% improve somewhat but need substantial support, 25% do not improve. Positive symptoms dominate early disability, negative symptoms chronic disability. Life expectancy is markedly reduced versus age-matched controls; suicide accounts for about 10%, while cardiovascular causes contribute most to excess mortality. Patients are more often victims than perpetrators of violence.

Detailed Notes

Opening and Lecturer's Background

• A consultant psychiatrist in Chennai, southern India, previously working many years in the UK; British training informs terminology and service approaches such as crisis intervention, home treatment and early intervention teams.

• Coverage: clinical features, ICD-10/DSM-5 classification, at-risk mental states, epidemiology, aetiology, assessment/management, prognosis, then five multiple-choice questions.

• About 52 minutes, a comprehensive single-disease overview. Slide lists such as eleven first-rank symptoms and antipsychotic side effects are not read item by item, leaving transcript gaps.

Name and Historical Development

• Greek roots mean “split mind,” referring to splitting of mental functions, entirely different from popular “split personality,” which is dissociative identity disorder (formerly multiple personality disorder).

• Coined by Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler in 1908 (transcribed "Eugene Boiler," restored from psychiatric history).

• Previously dementia praecox, popularised by Kraepelin ("ML Kreplin," meaning Emil Kraepelin), reflecting the view of early onset ending in deterioration.

Clinical Features

• Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder. Psychosis means experiences and/or beliefs lacking a basis in reality, principally hallucinations and delusions.

• Hallucination: sensory perception without corresponding stimulus, possible in all five modalities; auditory is commonest in psychosis (transcribed "audiary").

• Typically voices outside the head, third-person discussing the patient or second-person directly addressing them.

• Delusion: false fixed belief held with absolute conviction despite contrary evidence, not shared by family/cultural group—the last qualification distinguishes cultural/religious beliefs.

• Usually persecutory themes, e.g. “my neighbour is trying to poison me” or “cameras monitor my every move wherever I go”; sometimes grandiose.

• Eleven first-rank symptoms were enumerated by German psychiatrist Kurt Schneider, formerly considered diagnostic; no longer so because other psychoses show them, but they still strongly suggest schizophrenia.

• They include both hallucinations and delusions (listed on slides, not individually read; the lecturer refers viewers to Descriptive Psychopathology).

• Positive symptoms—hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder—occur acutely and respond relatively well to antipsychotics.

• Negative symptoms—poor motivation, reduced speech, poor self-care—occur chronically and generally respond poorly.

ICD-10 and DSM-5 Classification

• ICD-10 subtypes: paranoid, hebephrenic ("hepophrenic"), catatonic and simple.

• Paranoid is commonest clinically, with prominent delusions, hallucinations and thought disorder. Themes include persecution, reference, jealousy and grandeur; voices comment/discuss, threaten or command; somatic bodily-sensation or movement hallucinations also occur. Thought disorder produces incoherent, irrelevant speech or neologisms.

• Hebephrenic features inappropriate/incongruous affect, incoherent fragmented rambling speech and aimless rather than goal-directed behaviour. Delusions/hallucinations are absent or inconspicuous—the most practical distinction from paranoid illness.

• Catatonic stupor is most dramatic: mute and motionless. Other signs include posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, automatic obedience and catatonic excitement. A photograph illustrates posturing; another lecture covers catatonia in detail.

• Simple schizophrenia is predominantly negative: withdrawal, lost motivation, aimlessness, apathy, poverty of speech, marked social decline and absent positive symptoms.

• Lecture ICD-10 minimum durations: paranoid/hebephrenic one month, catatonic two weeks, simple one year. The last avoids mistaking personality change or declining function for illness.

• DSM-5 renames the category “schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders,” versus DSM-4's “schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders,” reflecting spectrum thinking.

• DSM-5 removes subtypes and uses symptom counts: two of five specified symptoms, at least one from the first three, with at least six months' duration. The five are listed but not read aloud, so the transcript lacks them.

• Symptoms lasting only 1–6 months belong to another category. Subtitles are missing except "schizophren..."; DSM-5 identifies this as schizophreniform disorder—explicitly a classification-based completion, not transcript wording.

• Another category raising future psychosis risk is mentioned as still being revised with research. Fragmentary subtitles prevent confirming its exact name; only its risk-increasing nature is clear.

At-Risk Mental State (ARMS)

• ARMS means at-risk mental state; related terms include ultra high-risk, subthreshold psychosis, attenuated psychosis and prodrome.

• ARMS and prodrome overlap but are distinct.

• ARMS is prospective: identify the state, follow individuals and observe development; only about one in three develops psychosis.

• If psychosis develops, the previous ARMS period retrospectively forms part of the prodrome—the connection between concepts.

• Prodrome is retrospective: after clear psychosis presents, look back for subtle changes preceding overt psychotic symptoms.

• Not all psychotic patients have a prodrome; its absence cannot exclude diagnosis.

Epidemiology

• Lifetime prevalence about 1%, annual incidence about 2/1000.

• Incidence varies between countries, within countries and even within cities.

• Male lifetime risk about 40% higher, ratio 1.4:1.

• Male onset peaks 15–24, women about 5–10 years later with a second peak (usually associated with perimenopause; the lecture states only that a second peak exists).

Aetiology

• Exact cause unknown; consensus favours interacting genetic/other biological, psychological and social factors.

• Biological factors probably outweigh psychological ones, a key aetiological contrast with neurotic disorders.

• A genetic component is established by family through genome-wide association studies, but no single causal gene found.

• Likely polygenic: many small-effect genes, shared with depression, bipolar disorder and developmental disorders such as autism.

• Genetic risk is neither necessary nor sufficient: illness can occur without known family history/risk genes; an identical co-twin sharing all genes may remain unaffected.

• Key risks: population 1%; monozygotic twin 50%; first-degree relatives 10%, tenfold population risk. More affected relatives means higher risk.

• Advanced paternal age associates with risk, perhaps via de novo mutations ("DNO mutations").

• 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, also DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome ("VOC cardioacial"), is the only established genetic subtype, only 1% of cases.

• Neurodevelopmental model: abnormal brain development years earlier, perhaps particularly apt for childhood-onset illness. Evidence includes macrostructural, microscopic and connectivity abnormalities.

• How much is causal versus consequences of illness/antipsychotic treatment remains debated.

• Obstetric complications during delivery and maternal pregnancy infections are commoner in patients' histories.

• Even at first diagnosis intracranial volume is reduced versus healthy controls, suggesting a process beginning years earlier; both white and grey matter decrease.

• With chronicity, white-matter loss stabilises but grey-matter loss progresses.

• Increased dopamine synthesis is detectable during the prodrome.

• NMDA receptor hypofunction ("hyperunction," context indicates hypofunction) seems earlier than dopamine abnormalities; “at least several years earlier” comes from the slide, with no years read explicitly.

• Low-grade inflammation with gliosis ("gyosis") is seen.

• Chronic illness shows reduced total brain volume and enlarged ventricles.

• None are specific changes in every patient; these are group comparisons with controls—important when explaining investigations to families.

• Childhood adversity is increasingly viewed as an important potential psychosocial risk.

• Migration is a risk, especially becoming a lower-socioeconomic ethnic minority in an affluent nation.

• Urban birth and major stressful life events also confer risk.

• Dopamine-enhancing substances can cause schizophrenia-like psychotic symptoms, usually resolving after cessation.

• Illicit drug use is commoner in schizophrenia; although drugs cause psychotic symptoms, they are unlikely truly to “cause” schizophrenia, but may bring onset forward in vulnerable individuals.

• Illicit drugs interfere with antipsychotic efficacy and increase relapse frequency.

• Some use is self-medication—illness causing drug use rather than vice versa; consider this causal direction.

• Epigenetics means environmentally induced gene “switching on/off,” changing expression without changing DNA sequence.

• Possible changes include methylation affecting GABA/BDNF genes and histone acetylation. These gene names are from the slide; the transcript's sentence begins incompletely with "…in genes in response to environmental".

• Animal studies suggest epigenetic changes can even pass to offspring.

• Psychoanalyst Frieda Fromm-Reichmann ("Freda from Reichman") proposed the “schizophrenogenic mother”: controlling, overprotective yet rejecting and insensitive treatment of children might cause schizophrenia.

• Gregory Bateson ("Gregory Batesson") proposed the related double-bind hypothesis; mainstream psychiatry no longer accepts either theory.

• A co-resident mother/close carer can nevertheless cause psychological harm through high expressed emotion. It does not cause schizophrenia but predisposes to relapse, revisited under prognosis.

Assessment and Management I: Assessment, Investigations and Risk

• First conduct thorough psychiatric examination and comprehensive medical history.

• Without specific indications, functional psychotic illness such as paranoid schizophrenia can be diagnosed confidently without unnecessary investigations.

• Supporting conditions: persistent, consistent psychotic symptoms for at least one month, especially after insomnia, irritability, suspiciousness and withdrawal as prodromal symptoms.

• Exclude illicit drugs, psychosis-inducing medication such as steroids and evidence of organic brain disease.

• No CT/MRI, EEG, psychometric/neuropsychological testing or structured personality questionnaires unless specifically indicated.

• Before treatment, routine blood tests, baseline ECG and urine drug screening if needed.

• Bloods/ECG matter because some atypicals increase glucose/lipids and prolong QTc; repeat at least every one to two years.

• Risk assessment is mandatory. Acute schizophrenia, especially early illness, raises suicide risk.

• Only a small minority poses risk to others, usually young men.

• Concerning symptoms include commands to harm self/others and delusions of external control.

• Violence risks: past violence, comorbid alcohol/substance misuse, medication non-adherence, antisocial traits and poor insight.

• Patients are likelier violence victims than perpetrators; even when violent, targets are likelier acquaintances than strangers.

Assessment and Management II: Principles, Antipsychotics and Clozapine

• Antipsychotics, also called neuroleptics, are the main treatment.

• Where available, add CBT for treatment-resistant psychotic symptoms.

• Acute illness may require admission, sometimes involuntary, based on severity, poor insight, potential risk and no reliable home carer.

• Severe chronic illness requires long-term psychosocial rehabilitation.

• The dopamine hypothesis underlies antipsychotics: excess brain dopamine activity causes schizophrenia, so reducing it treats illness.

• They block postsynaptic dopamine receptors, preventing dopamine action.

• Despite many shortcomings of the hypothesis, all licensed schizophrenia drugs are considered effective through normalising dopamine activity.

• Older/first-generation/typical drugs include chlorpromazine ("chloroprozine") and haloperidol; newer/second-generation drugs are atypicals.

• They may also be classified by route/duration, e.g. long-acting injections versus oral preparations.

• Typical/atypical efficacy is broadly similar despite some contrary studies; adverse effects mainly distinguish them.

• Extrapyramidal effects are much commoner with older non-selective dopamine antagonists and strongly contribute to non-adherence.

• Metabolic effects are commoner with some newer drugs, such as clozapine.

• Individualise choice. General lecture rule: start new patients on atypicals; do not switch a successful, well-tolerated older drug used for years unnecessarily.

• Clozapine is superior for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

• Resistance means failure of at least two different adequate-dose, adequate-duration antipsychotics, affecting about 20–30%.

• Clozapine causes agranulocytosis in about 1% (transcribed "granuloccytosis"), so is not first-line.

• Regular white-cell/neutrophil monitoring follows local/national guidelines.

• Its anti-suicide effect is an important distinguishing clinical benefit.

Assessment and Management III: Prescribing, Duration and Maintenance

• “Start low and go slow”: begin low and gradually increase if needed.

• The lecturer's experience is that many respond well below manufacturer-recommended doses.

• Review mental state, monitor side effects and avoid antipsychotic polypharmacy—more than one concurrently.

• Antipsychotic effects take at least 2–3 weeks to begin, another 2–3 to peak.

• Continue months after recovery if improving; switch if not improving.

• Repeated relapse whenever medication stops suggests long-term maintenance; if non-adherence drives relapse, consider depot injections monthly, fortnightly, etc.

• Initially choose outpatient versus inpatient care by severity and risk.

• Start one atypical selected by side effects, preferences, medical history and previous response.

• If not the first episode, start low and adjust to effects/adverse effects.

• Use an adequate dose for at least 4–6 weeks for optimum effect.

• In the first days add benzodiazepines for agitation/restlessness or hypnotics for insomnia if needed, not as routine long-term prescriptions.

• Continue antipsychotics at least one year after remission.

• After failure of an adequate first drug, switch atypicals while assessing adherence, alcohol/drug misuse, interactions and psychosocial stressors as possible causes of “failure.”

• If a second fails, consider clozapine.

• In some countries crisis intervention/home treatment teams substitute for admission; early intervention teams manage the first years.

• Maintenance has three aims: sustained symptom control, reduced relapse and improved quality of life/function.

• Duration depends on episode number, severity and functional impact.

• Rule of thumb after remission: first episode at least one year, second two years, third/subsequent five years; some require lifelong treatment.

• If stable for the required period and doctor/patient decide to stop, taper to prevent rebound relapse.

Assessment and Management IV: Side Effects, EPS and NMS

• Main atypicals: risperidone ("respiranzipine"), quetiapine ("quitapene"), aripiprazole ("ariprazole") and olanzapine ("toapine").

• Except aripiprazole, atypicals are D2 antagonists; all also antagonise 5HT2A.

• Aripiprazole partially agonises D2 and 5HT1A, its mechanistic distinction.

• Clozapine has greater D4 affinity than D1/D2/D3/D5.

• A complete adverse-effect slide is shown; not every drug causes every listed effect (pause to record).

• NMS can occur with any antipsychotic, commoner with older high-potency agents ("hypotensy").

• EPS results from nigrostriatal dopamine blockade ("nigro triatital"), commoner with older typicals.

• Acute EPS includes dystonia and akathisia, described in the lecture as responding well to anticholinergics such as procyclidine.

• Chronic EPS includes parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia.

• As noted, non-selective older drugs such as haloperidol produce far more EPS than more selective newer drugs.

• Tardive dyskinesia features involuntary orofacial movements, with choreiform movements in severe cases.

• Risks: age, pre-existing organic brain disease, female sex, high-potency drugs and long treatment duration.

• Mechanism thought to be dopamine-receptor supersensitivity.

• Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia and should be avoided in it.

• NMS is an idiosyncratic antipsychotic reaction: hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability and clouding of consciousness.

• Bloods show raised creatine phosphokinase and neutrophilic leucocytosis.

• Best managed in a general medical ward or ICU.

• Catatonic patients have high NMS risk with antipsychotics; hence these are avoided during catatonia, even with underlying schizophrenia, until that phase passes.

• Principal concern is renal failure from rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria.

• Options include supportive care, benzodiazepines, dantrolene, bromocriptine and ECT in severe cases.

• Newer atypicals: paliperidone, iloperidone, asenapine and lurasidone.

• Like most earlier atypicals, these antagonise D2 and 5HT2A.

Assessment and Management V: Non-Drug Treatments, ECT and Recovery

• Adjuncts to antipsychotics: psychoeducation, CBT, family therapy/intervention, art therapy, adherence therapy, cognitive remediation and social skills training.

• The lecture gives catatonic schizophrenia as the only ECT indication in schizophrenia.

• ECT augmentation of clozapine for resistance may become an indication, with promising results, but larger, longer trials are needed before confident recommendation.

• The recovery model has gained recognition over the past decade or more.

• It centres the patient, unlike traditional clinician-centred care where patients passively receive treatment.

• Recovery is a journey rather than a particular outcome.

• It includes social recovery, not merely symptom recovery.

• Core concepts include hope, empowerment and meaning.

• Interestingly, patients in low/middle-income countries seem to recover better than those in affluent countries despite no formal recovery-service model.

Prognosis

• Good factors: female sex, acute onset, clear precipitating event, prominent affective symptoms, early treatment, good response, good premorbid occupational adjustment and stable family circumstances.

• Poor factors: early onset, insidious onset, long untreated psychosis, prominent negative symptoms, premorbid personality difficulties, comorbid alcohol/drug misuse and high expressed emotion.

• High expressed emotion means emotional overinvolvement, hostility and critical comments.

• Living in such a family increases relapse (specific examples on the slide).

• Family therapy and day hospitals, allowing daytime away from home, may help.

• Old “rule of thirds”: one-third fully recover, one-third improve over time, one-third do not improve.

• Refined “rule of quarters”: 25% fully recover without long-term treatment; 25% improve well and live independently; 25% improve somewhat but need substantial additional support; 25% no improvement.

• The final group may need recurrent admissions for positive symptoms or long institutional rehabilitation for negative symptoms.

• Positive symptoms cause most early impairment, negative symptoms most chronic impairment.

• Life expectancy is markedly reduced versus age-matched controls: suicide (about 10%), lifestyle, acute symptoms, chronic low motivation preventing physical help-seeking, intentional/unintentional discrimination by other clinicians and metabolic medication effects such as diabetes, weight/lipid gain.

• Overall cardiovascular causes contribute most to excess mortality.

Five Self-Test MCQs

See “Self-Test MCQs and Answers” below for the five closing questions.

Scales and Assessment Tools

• PANSS (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale): Commonest schizophrenia research scale, observer-rated, 30 items across positive, negative and general psychopathology, each scored 0–6 in the lecture.

• BPRS (Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale): Another scale; no item count, score range or cut-off supplied.

• The lecture stresses scales are required neither to diagnose nor monitor progress in practice; mainly research tools.

• No other screening tools, structured interviews or cut-offs covered.

Prescribing and duration points:

• Starting: “Start low, go slow”; many respond well below manufacturer doses.

• Timing: At least 2–3 weeks to onset, another 2–3 to peak; adequate dose at least 4–6 weeks for best response.

• Switching: Adequate first atypical fails → another atypical (check adherence, alcohol/drugs, interactions, psychosocial stress) → if second fails consider clozapine.

• After remission: At least one year; maintenance first episode one year, second two, third/subsequent five, sometimes lifelong; taper against rebound relapse.

• Depots: When non-adherence drives relapse, monthly/fortnightly etc.

• Adjuncts: Benzodiazepines/hypnotics initially, not routinely long term.

• Avoid polypharmacy: Avoid multiple concurrent antipsychotics.

• Special warning: Catatonia increases antipsychotic NMS risk; wait until it passes.

• ECT: Sole lecture indication catatonic schizophrenia; clozapine augmentation may become an indication but evidence insufficient.

• Psychosocial interventions: Psychoeducation, CBT, family therapy/intervention, art, adherence, cognitive remediation and social skills; severe chronic illness needs long rehabilitation; recovery stresses hope, empowerment, meaning and social recovery.

• Services: Crisis/home treatment alternatives to admission; early intervention in initial years.

• Monitoring: Pretreatment routine bloods/ECG, urine drug screen if needed; repeat bloods/ECG at least every 1–2 years due to glucose/lipid/QTc risks; regular white-cell/neutrophil counts with clozapine.

Self-Test MCQs and Answers

Q1: What suggests hebephrenic rather than paranoid schizophrenia?

• Answer: Incongruous affect.

• Explanation: Other three favour paranoid illness. Key hebephrenic features: inappropriate/incongruous affect, fragmented speech, aimless behaviour and inconspicuous delusions/hallucinations. Other options not read aloud.

Q2: Which is not a characteristic clozapine adverse effect?

• Answer: Hyperprolactinaemia.

• Explanation: Clozapine does not cause it; the other three are characteristic, but their names cannot be supplied because options are not read.

Q3: Which statement about schizophrenia genetics is correct?

• Answer: Option two—polygenic, involving many genes of individually small effect.

• Explanation: One is false because genetics matters substantially; three false because 22q11.2 deletion accounts for only 1%. First-degree risk is actually tenfold: population 1%, relatives 10%. Original options unread.

Q4: Which is not a poor prognostic factor?

• Answer: Acute onset—a good factor.

• Explanation: Other three are poor factors, options unread. Lecture list includes early/insidious onset, long untreated psychosis, prominent negatives, premorbid personality difficulties, substance misuse and high expressed emotion.

Q5: Which atypical does not primarily act by D2 antagonism: aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone?

• Answer: Aripiprazole.

• Explanation: A partial D2 agonist; the other three antagonists. Transcript "alanzipene" restored contextually to olanzapine, explicitly a recognition correction, not transcript wording.

Key Quotations

"The word schizophrenia is derived from Greek and it literally means split mind. However, it is important to realize that schizophrenia is different from multiple personality disorder which is a dissociative identity disorder."

“Schizophrenia is Greek for ‘split mind,’ but differs from multiple personality/dissociative identity disorder.”

"They are no longer considered diagnostic of schizophrenia as they can occur in psychotic conditions other than schizophrenia also. But the presence of these symptoms strongly suggests a diagnosis of schizophrenia."

“First-rank symptoms are no longer diagnostic since other psychoses have them, but their presence strongly suggests schizophrenia.”

"It is likely that genetic risk is neither necessary nor sufficient for schizophrenia."

“Genetic risk is probably neither necessary nor sufficient.”

"So start low and go slow."

“Start at a low dose and increase slowly.”

"Patients are more likely to be victims of violence rather than being perpetrators of violence."

“Patients are more likely victims than perpetrators of violence.”

"Overall, cardiovascular causes are the single biggest contributor to the increased mortality that is seen in patients with schizophrenia."

“Cardiovascular causes are the largest single contributor to excess schizophrenia mortality.”

Commonly Confused Concepts

• Schizophrenia vs multiple personality/dissociative identity disorder: “Split mind” means divided mental functions, not personality division. Patients/families often confuse them; clarify the name first.

• ARMS vs prodrome: ARMS looks forward, identifies then follows, with only one-third converting; prodrome looks back from diagnosed psychosis to subtle changes, not present in everyone. Mnemonic: ARMS forward, prodrome backward.

• Positive vs negative: Positives (hallucinations/delusions/thought disorder) acute, medication-responsive, dominate early disability; negatives (low motivation/speech/self-care) chronic, poorly responsive, dominate chronic disability.

• ICD-10 minimum subtype durations: Paranoid/hebephrenic one month, catatonic two weeks, simple one year. The more diagnosis depends on absent positives, the longer observation; one year for simple excludes personality change/functional decline.

• Acute EPS vs tardive dyskinesia: Lecture describes dystonia/akathisia as anticholinergic-responsive; tardive orofacial movements reflect receptor supersensitivity and worsen with anticholinergics, which must be avoided.

• Typical vs atypical: Similar efficacy, differing adverse effects—EPS/NMS commoner with non-selective older drugs, metabolic effects with some newer ones such as clozapine. Start new patients atypical, but do not switch effective well-tolerated longstanding older treatment unnecessarily.

• Identical twins 50%, first-degree relatives 10%, population 1%: Know all three; 50% shows genetics matters but is insufficient, since a genetically identical twin can remain well.

Clinical Application / Memory Anchors

• Three treatment steps: “Start low, go slow → adequate dose 4–6 weeks → at least one year after remission”; remember “2–3 weeks to onset, another 2–3 to peak.”

• Maintenance ladder: First episode one year, second two, third/subsequent five, sometimes lifelong; taper against rebound.

• Resistance and solution: Two adequate trials fail (20–30%) → clozapine → remember 1% agranulocytosis, regular white-cell/neutrophil counts and anti-suicide effects.

• Investigations: Functional psychosis needs no CT/MRI, EEG or neuropsychology unless indicated; pretreatment bloods + ECG + urine screen if needed; bloods/ECG at least every 1–2 years.

• Catatonia/antipsychotic boundary: High NMS risk (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, clouded consciousness, raised CPK/neutrophils); wait until catatonia passes. Catatonic schizophrenia is the lecture's sole ECT indication.

• Prognosis/mortality: Thirds refined to quarters (25% recovered/25% independent/25% substantial support/25% no improvement). Reduced life expectancy, suicide 10%, but cardiovascular disease the largest single mortality contributor—glucose, lipids and weight monitoring are themselves treatment.

• Two risk-communication sentences: Patients are more often violence victims than perpetrators; nevertheless command voices and control delusions require immediate risk assessment.
